title: The deer in the hermitage
hook: hermits stop a king's arrow, and in their grove the deer don't run
carry: where non-harm takes root, hostility drops

segments.voice: Yesterday: niyama, the second limb, and tapas, discipline offered to God, in Parvati's fire. Today, what grows when the restraints take root.

A king is out hunting, standing in his chariot, an arrow already on the string. Ahead of him a deer runs for its life, glancing back over its shoulder. He's about to shoot when voices call out: king, stop! This deer belongs to the hermitage. Hermits step into the path with their hands raised. And the king, the most powerful man in the forest, lowers his bow. This is the opening of Kalidasa's play Shakuntala. As King Dushyanta walks on into the grove, he notices something strange: here, the deer don't run from the sound of his chariot.
screen: `AN ARROW ON THE STRING.` → `THIS DEER BELONGS TO THE HERMITAGE.` → `THE KING LOWERS HIS BOW.`

segments.voice: Hindu stories picture hermitages this way again and again: places where animals stop being afraid and hunters stop hunting. Patanjali puts that picture into one sutra. Sutra 2.35: when someone is grounded in non-harm, hostility is given up in their presence. Not their own hostility. Everyone else's. Grounded means firmly established, standing on it. The classical commentary says all creatures near such a person abandon their enmity. Then come the fruits of the other four restraints. Grounded in truth, your words don't fail. Grounded in not stealing, jewels come near. Grounded in restraint, vigor. Grounded in not grasping, insight into the how and why of your births. How should these be read? Within the tradition, some take them as real powers that come with mastery. Others read them as the natural shape of a life: people drop their guard around someone who will never hurt them, and trust the word of someone who never lies. Both readings agree on one thing. The fruit doesn't come from chasing the fruit. The hermits didn't train the deer to be brave. Their way of living did it, over years. You may have met someone like that: a grandmother who sits down at a dinner that's about to turn into a fight, asks someone about their garden, and the air changes. She isn't performing calm. She stopped carrying a weapon a long time ago.
screen: `A GROVE WHERE DEER DON'T RUN.` · `AROUND NON-HARM, HOSTILITY DROPS.` · `TRUTH: WORDS THAT DON'T FAIL.` · `POWERS, OR THE SHAPE OF A LIFE?` · then, large: `THE FRUITS OF THE YAMAS.`

segments.voice: Picture the next room you'll walk into, a kitchen, an office, a group chat, and notice whether you're carrying anything sharp: a grievance, a comeback, a scorecard. Set it down for the length of this sit, the way you'd leave a heavy bag by the door. Breathe as someone with nothing to defend.
Vaira-tyaga, the giving up of hostility that happens around one grounded in non-harm. The first of five fruits that come when the restraints are fully rooted.
Your line: where non-harm takes root, hostility drops. The hermits never fought the king; their way of life lowered his bow. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu stories, from Kalidasa's Shakuntala to the Puranas, often describe hermitages as places where wild animals live at peace, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present the fruits of 2.35–2.39 as signs that the restraints have taken root, whether read as powers or as the natural results of an ethical life.

original.note: Sanskrit vaira-tyāga: vaira (hostility, enmity) plus tyāga (giving up); the fruit of non-harm in 2.35.
